title: Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution: MSBuild
shortTitle: Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution: MSBuild
summary: MSBuild is the Microsoft Build Engine, a signed Microsoft executable that reads XML project files and builds the platforms and configurations they describe. This sub-technique covers its use as an execution proxy rather than as a build tool. The central abuse is the inline task, a .NET feature that allows C sharp or Visual Basic code to be written directly inside the project file; MSBuild compiles that code in memory and runs it, so no payload binary is written to disk for a scanner to find. Because msbuild.exe is signed and typically permitted by application control policy, the code inherits that trust. Defenders see the build engine started with a project file from an unusual path, very often a temporary or downloads directory or a remote share, and frequently as a child of a document reader, a script host or a scheduled task. Build servers run it constantly, so the discriminators are the parent, the project path and the absence of any real source repository.

beginner.definition: MSBuild is a Microsoft program that builds software from a project file. The project file is written in XML, a text format that uses tags to describe settings. The parent technique covers trusted developer tools in general. This sub-technique is the MSBuild case, where the build engine itself runs the attacker's code.
beginner.whyItMatters: MSBuild is signed by Microsoft, so security tools usually allow it to run. It can compile and run code that is written inside the project file itself. So no separate program file is needed at all. This lets an attacker run code on a machine that blocks unknown programs. In a task list, the build tool looks completely normal.
howItWorks: The attacker writes an XML project file that contains an inline task. An inline task is a block of code stored inside that file.
The code inside the inline task is written in C sharp or Visual Basic, two common Microsoft programming languages.
MSBuild reads the project file, compiles the inline task in memory, and runs the resulting code.
No separate program file is written to disk, so file based scanning may find nothing at all.
The tool is signed by Microsoft, so application control rules that allow it are still satisfied.
In real cases the project file is often opened from a temporary folder, a downloads folder or a remote share.
beginner.example: Imagine an office where only the photocopier is allowed to make copies. Somebody slides a sheet into it with instructions written in the margin. The machine reads the margin and follows the instructions, because margin notes are part of how it normally works. The security guard only checked that the machine was allowed into the room.
takeaways: This sub-technique is the build engine case, where the trusted tool is MSBuild itself.
Inline tasks let code live inside the project file, so nothing is written to disk.
A project file loaded from a temporary, downloads or network folder is the strongest clue.

objectives: Explain what MSBuild is and what a project file contains.
Describe how an inline task runs code without dropping a file on disk.
Explain how this sub-technique differs from its parent technique.
Identify process and command line evidence of MSBuild abuse.
Explain why application control rules that allow MSBuild carry risk.
